newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher, boosted by Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher, boosted by Greenspan.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher on Friday, as Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks were taken to mean the Fed is mostly pleased with the economy's performance and may not have to raise interest rates much more -- if at all.

Greenspan, speaking in New York on Thursday night, defended the Fed's quarter-point rate hike in March. He said that while he expects economic growth to slow later this year and into next year, the Fed would act again should growth remain strong.
"The market has the sense (the Fed) is either not going at all or just one more time and that's it," said Jim Nealis, head trader at PaineWebber Inc.

As such, Treasuries rejoiced somewhat, pushing prices up as much as 5/8-point during overseas trading during the night. Treasuries came off their highs, but the 30-year bond was still up a half-point at 96-19/32, to yield 6.89 percent.
The two-year note, meanwhile, was at 100-7/32, up 4/32, to yield 6.25 percent.
Nealis noted that the buying thus far this session was "real," coming from central banks and domestic accounts.
For the most part, players said they still anticipate another tightening, but whether it comes at the Fed's policy setting meeting later this month or early July is subject to debate.
Greenspan said that the March move was an insurance policy against future inflation.
"His tone was defensive," said one head trader at a large U.S. bank/dealer of Greenspan's remarks. "That means (more) pre-emptive tightening."
Adds Larry Dyer, government bond strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston: "They're still poised to go if we don't slow," he said.
However, Dyer said Greenspan's speech should have "been more aggressive if he planned to go in May, I think that's the general tone of the market.

"I started looking at it with an expectation that May was unlikely, then people started looking at as such May was more likely and now less," he said. "That can send us up a bit but I don't think that it takes us out of a Fed tightening environment."

In the absence of economic data this session, market participants said Treasuries should bounce around in a trading range, and retain the early gains -- and perhaps grind higher -- if the buying seen overnight continues.
Nealis said that technicals are good and dealer positions are small. He added that the market awaits remarks from San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry, who speaks at 1030 EDT/1430 GMT in Oregon.
"It's hard to top Greenspan," he said. "But (Parry) may have his own flavor and a second message from Greenspan."
